en: The Sixteen-Verse Instruction on Phonetics:
Now I shall proclaim the rule for the pronunciation of speech, as it was spoken by the Self-Existent One himself for the purposes of worldly communication. (1)
There are thirty-three consonants (*varṇa*), twenty-two vowels (*svara*), four *yamas*, and one each for *visarga* and *anusvāra*; thus, there are sixty-three [phonemes].
Among these, those ending in *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* are to be known as short (*samā*), while *ṛ* with a long vowel (*dīrgha*) has *ḷ* as its fifth [corresponding short vowel].
The four vowels *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* are diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) and are not short (*ahrasva*).

Their distinctions are short, long, and protracted (*pluta*); they are also acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*); and they are both nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*ananunāsika*). 3–4.

Thus, there are eighteen distinct vowel-sounds (*nāmin*): the vowels (*svara*) and the consonant groups *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *va*; this is the collection of the five classes of sounds. These are the distinctions of the vowels.
[The consonants] beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are derived from the fifth letter of each group in reverse order.

The letters beginning with *kha* and *pha* are to be known as *cha*, *ṭha*, and *tha*; those ending with *ra* and *la* are remembered as *ha*, *ya*, and *va*. Following these are the vowels (*svara*), and then the consonants (*hal*):
*ña-ma*, *jha-bha*, *ja-va*, *kha-tha*, *ca-pa*, and *śa-sa*; these are the numerous *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated) groups.

The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are the *sparśa* (contact) letters; *ya*, *ma*, *ja*, *bha*, and *ña* are the *antaḥsthā* (semivowels); *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are the *ūṣman* (sibilants); and *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are known as the *antaḥsthā*. Prior to *kha* and *pha* respectively, there are the half-*visarga* (*arddha-visarga*) sounds.
The *jihvāmūlīya* is to be known as that which has the name *upadhmanīya*.
The *visarga*, half-*visarga*, *anusvāra*, and the unmanifest (*vyaṅga*) depend on what follows.
These [consonants] are "prior" (*para*) and "subsequent" (*apara*), while the short vowels *ka* and *la* are light, and the long vowel is likewise heavy.

Thus are the distinctions of the articulate sounds (*vyaṅga*): *ha*, *k*, and the *visarjanīya* are guttural; *y*, *i*, *ś*, and *c* are palatal; *ṛ*, *ṭ*, *u*, *ṣ*, and *r* are retroflex; *l*, *t*, and *u* are dental; and the two *upadhmānīya*s are labial. (11)

The sound *va* is produced at the teeth and lips; *ña*, *ma*, and *ya* are produced at the nose; *u*, *da*, and *au* are produced at the throat and lips; *t* and *e* are produced at the throat and palate;
and for the *jihvāmūlīya* alone, the root of the tongue is indeed the eighth [place of articulation].
The instruction that brings about immediate awakening has been revealed as a jewel.
(13) One who is hideous, or has a hanging lip, or is indistinct, or nasal, or stammers, or has a bound tongue, is not fit to utter the application [of the mantra]. (14)

Just as a tigress, fearing harm from being caught or crushed, would carry her cubs with her teeth, so too should one employ the phonemes; by that means, one is glorified in the world. (15) Thus ends the section on the pronunciation of the phonemes.
Whoever, being self-restrained, recites here this instruction issued by Śiva,
shall possess sons, fame, wealth, and long life, and enjoy supreme happiness in heaven.
Thus ends the *Ṣoḍaśaślokī-śikṣā* composed by Rāmakṛṣṇa.
